Erdős problem #1049

Lambert-type series at rational bases

For which rational bases is the corresponding series irrational? The first resistant explicit base is three halves.

Open Problem on GitHub
ResultsPapersLean mapWhat is checked

Results and open questions

#1049. For positive integers 0 <𝑏 <𝑎0<b<a in the exact Zudilin contour region, Lean checks irrationality and the stated irrationality-exponent bound for 𝐹(𝑎/𝑏)F(a/b), including every positive integral power of 31/431/4. The short paper also gives an ordinary proof for coprime 𝑎,𝑏a,b under log⁡𝑏/log⁡𝑎 <𝜃∗log⁡b/log⁡a<θ∗, where 𝜃∗ ≈0.4056830214θ∗≈0.4056830214, using Zudilin’s 2004 forms and estimates. Zudilin’s prior work is credited; formalisation does not establish novelty. Lean also checks the normalized Hankel determinant’s order and leading coefficient at every rank.

Separately, for each real 𝑝 >1p>1 and 1 ≤𝑁 ≤81≤N≤8, the Lean-checked finite coefficient pencil has a positive definite first matrix, real roots strictly below 𝐹(𝑝)F(p), and non-strict interlacing at adjacent ranks. The eight unshifted determinant certificates are kernel checked; the shifted eight and 76 cyclotomic residue witnesses remain finite computations. These results give no all-rank coefficient positivity or irrationality at 3/23/2, which lies outside the contour region. The universal rational-base question remains open. Read the short paper, long record, and selected formal checks.

The prepared E1049_01 Comparator selection contains 25 rational-base contour and measure declarations, including rational_base_threshold. It does not select the later Hankel determinant or finite coefficient-pencil results in the same paper. The caller-side preflight passed at that exact source commit; no registry intake is claimed.

Introduction

For 𝑡 >1t>1, expansion of each geometric series gives

𝐹(𝑡)=∑𝑛≥11𝑡𝑛−1=∑𝑛≥1𝜏(𝑛)𝑡𝑛,F(t)=∑n≥11tn−1=∑n≥1τ(n)tn,

where 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) is the number of positive divisors of 𝑛n. With 𝑞 =1/𝑡q=1/t, this is the 𝑞q-harmonic series ∑𝑛≥1𝑞𝑛/(1 −𝑞𝑛)∑n≥1qn/(1−qn). The rearrangement is justified by nonnegativity, and the resulting series converges since 𝜏(𝑛) ≤𝑛τ(n)≤n and ∑𝑛≥1𝑛𝑡−𝑛 <∞∑n≥1nt−n<∞.

Chowla conjectured that 𝐹(𝑡)F(t) is irrational for every rational 𝑡 >1t>1, as Erdős records ; this is Erdős Problem #1049. The conjecture remains open. We prove a sufficient condition on the numerator and denominator of 𝑡t, using Zudilin’s 2004 construction [4]. The condition includes 31/431/4 and every positive integral power of 31/431/4 (proved in Lean), and it excludes 3/23/2 (also proved in Lean).

The extra difficulty at a rational base is the denominator. If 𝑈,𝑉 ∈ℤ[𝑋]U,V∈Z[X] have degree at most 𝑊W, then 𝑏𝑊𝑈(𝑎/𝑏)bWU(a/b) and 𝑏𝑊𝑉(𝑎/𝑏)bWV(a/b) are integers. To prove irrationality by these forms, their positive remainders 𝑈(𝑎/𝑏)𝐹(𝑎/𝑏) −𝑉(𝑎/𝑏)U(a/b)F(a/b)−V(a/b) must remain small after multiplication by 𝑏𝑊bW.

A small example shows why cancellation should come first. At 3/23/2, the pair (𝑋 +1)(𝑋 +2),(𝑋 +1)(𝑋 +3)(X+1)(X+2),(X+1)(X+3), cleared with degree bound 22, gives (35,45)(35,45). Cancelling 𝑋 +1X+1 in the polynomial ring and then using degree bound 11 gives (7,9)(7,9). The example is not an approximation to 𝐹F; it illustrates how a common polynomial factor changes the required power of the denominator. For Zudilin’s polynomials the corresponding factors are cyclotomic, and their degrees determine the cutoff below.

For the cancelled polynomials 𝑈𝑛,𝑉𝑛Un,Vn used here, put Λ𝑛 =𝑈𝑛𝐹 −𝑉𝑛Λn=UnF−Vn and 𝑊𝑛 =deg⁡𝑈𝑛Wn=deg⁡Un. We prove deg⁡𝑉𝑛 =𝑊𝑛 −1deg⁡Vn=Wn−1 and

log(𝑏𝑊𝑛Λ𝑛(𝑎/𝑏))=(𝐶1log⁡𝑏−𝐶0log⁡𝑎)𝑛2+𝑜(𝑛2),log(bWnΛn(a/b))=(C1log⁡b−C0log⁡a)n2+o(n2),

where 𝐶0,𝐶1C0,C1 are defined below. If the coefficient of 𝑛2n2 is negative, the forms have integer coefficients and positive values tending to zero. If 𝐹(𝑎/𝑏)F(a/b) were rational, multiplying by its fixed denominator would give positive integers tending to zero, a contradiction.

The proof of the rational-base result occupies Section 2. The independent argument in Section 3 computes the first nonzero term of a Hankel determinant from the 2016 construction. Neither proof uses Section 4, which records supplementary tests for congruence-based arguments at 3/23/2. The companion Zudilin’s Forms at Rational Bases: Proofs and Research Record, called the long record below, gives the additional moment calculations, source comparisons and computational certificates.

Links in the running text go to Lean proofs of single steps, such as a finite inequality; such a link does not cover the surrounding argument.

Theorem 2.1 (rational-base region for Zudilin’s forms). Let 𝑎 >𝑏 ≥1a>b≥1 be coprime integers with

𝑏𝜇<𝑎,equivalentlylog⁡𝑏log⁡𝑎<𝜃∗,𝜃∗=𝐶0𝐶1=0.4056830213840605…,𝜇=𝐶1𝐶0=2.4649786835749750….bμ<a,equivalentlylog⁡blog⁡a<θ∗,θ∗=C0C1=0.4056830213840605…,μ=C1C0=2.4649786835749750….

The condition holds for every integer base, since 𝑏 =1b=1 gives log⁡𝑏/log⁡𝑎 =0log⁡b/log⁡a=0. For a fixed denominator 𝑏 >1b>1, it requires 𝑎 >𝑏2.46497868…a>b2.46497868…, much more than 𝑎 >𝑏a>b; nevertheless it gives infinitely many reduced noninteger rational bases for each such 𝑏b. The base 31/431/4 satisfies the condition, and taking a common positive integer power of the numerator and denominator leaves their logarithmic ratio unchanged. The base 3/23/2 is excluded since 𝜃∗ <1/2 <log⁡2/log⁡3θ∗<1/2<log⁡2/log⁡3. At equality log⁡𝑏/log⁡𝑎 =𝜃∗log⁡b/log⁡a=θ∗ the quadratic exponent vanishes, so the estimates below give no conclusion.

Formal sources.

The Lean proofs of Theorem 2.1 and its two corollaries construct the cancelled coefficient polynomials and prove the remainder estimates. Of Zudilin’s two constructions , the argument here uses the 2004 forms; Section 3 uses the 2016 sequence.

The first nonzero term of Zudilin’s Hankel determinant

The order of a nonzero formal series is its least exponent with nonzero coefficient. Matrix-entry orders alone give only a lower bound for the determinant, because terms can cancel. Here a moment expansion has a unique least-order term. We work in formal power series; values at a fixed real 𝑞q require a separate estimate.

Here 𝑁N denotes the Hankel rank and 𝑞q is a formal variable. At 𝑥 =𝑧 =1x=z=1, Zudilin’s normalised moments [5] are

What neither calculation implies.

Theorem 3.2 replaces that band by explicit linear and logarithmic terms and a constant. It changes no cubic coefficient and no prime-power valuation, so it supplies no divisor for the 2004 polynomial forms. Against the two proposed degree savings of long Section 3, the shortfall at 3/23/2 is exactly 𝑁(74𝑁2 −117𝑁 +41)/41 >0N(74N2−117N+41)/41>0 for 𝑁 ≥2N≥2, and the new estimate closes no part of it. Neither assertion supplies the cyclotomic divisibility proved for a different recurrence in [14]. Long Section 3.3 gives the separate coefficient and content calculations; Appendix A separates its fixed-rank Lean results from its finite computations.

Supplementary arithmetic at 3/23/2

The principal proofs are complete. The question here is whether combinations of evaluated rows can be divided by a common integer without losing nonvanishing or smallness of the remainder. This is a different operation from the polynomial cancellation in Section 2. The results below give necessary tests and conditional counting arguments, not such a family.

Primitive integer rows are unimodular modulo every modulus: for (2,3)(2,3) modulo 66, neither coordinate is a unit, but −2 +3 =1−2+3=1. Vanishing minors is an extra assumption. It is imposed in the quotient ring, not in ℤZ: the rows (1,0),(1,6)(1,0),(1,6) below have determinant 66 and coincide modulo 66. Arbitrary primitive rows need not satisfy it; (1,0),(0,1)(1,0),(0,1) have determinant 11. No such approximation family is constructed here.

Proposition 4.8 (rescaling two integer rows). Multiplying two integer rows by 𝑐1c1 and 𝑐2c2 multiplies their determinant by 𝑐1𝑐2c1c2. The integer identity and its absolute-value form show that the added divisibility is accompanied by exactly the same factor in the real absolute value.

For nonzero row contents 𝑐1,𝑐2c1,c2, write 𝑟𝑖 =𝑐𝑖𝑟prim𝑖ri=ciriprim. Then det(𝑟1,𝑟2) =𝑐1𝑐2det(𝑟prim1,𝑟prim2)det(r1,r2)=c1c2det(r1prim,r2prim) and 𝑟𝑖 ⋅(𝜉, −1) =𝑐𝑖𝑟prim𝑖 ⋅(𝜉, −1)ri⋅(ξ,−1)=ciriprim⋅(ξ,−1). These identities concern multiplication or division of whole integer rows, not cancellation of a polynomial factor before specialisation. Nor does dividing different rows by different contents preserve a fixed residue relation: (1,1) +(5,5)(1,1)+(5,5) is zero modulo 66, but the sum of the primitive rows is (2,2)(2,2). Even contents coprime to the modulus require the residue map to be formed again after row-by-row normalisation.

Residue counts and the index after division

The primitive rows (1,0),(1,6)(1,0),(1,6) generate ℤ ⊕6ℤZ⊕6Z. Modulo 22 this lattice has only two residue vectors, but dividing its even vectors by 22 gives ℤ ⊕3ℤZ⊕3Z, which still has index 33 in ℤ2Z2. Thus a small residue space need not become the full integer lattice after division. Smith normal form gives both quantities in general.

Let a rank-two lattice Λ ⊂ℤ2Λ⊂Z2 be generated by primitive rows, and let 𝑔 >0g>0 be the gcd of their 2 ×22×2 minors. By the description of Smith invariants through gcds of minors , its Smith invariants are 1,𝑔1,g. For 𝐷 ≥1D≥1, therefore

| | |im⁡(Λmod𝐷)| | |=𝐷2gcd(𝑔,𝐷),[ℤ2:Λ∩𝐷ℤ2𝐷]=𝑔gcd(𝑔,𝐷).|im⁡(ΛmodD)|=D2gcd(g,D),[Z2:Λ∩DZ2D]=ggcd(g,D).

A unimodular change of coordinates preserves 𝐷ℤ2DZ2 and reduces both calculations to ℤ ⊕𝑔ℤZ⊕gZ. Thus, when 𝐷 ∣𝑔D∣g, there are only 𝐷D residues, but the divided lattice still has index 𝑔/𝐷g/D. The general formulas without primitive generators are in the long record, Section 10.1.

If two independent divided rows (𝐴𝑖,𝐵𝑖)(Ai,Bi) have |𝐴𝑖| ≤𝐻|Ai|≤H and |𝐴𝑖𝜉 −𝐵𝑖| ≤𝜀|Aiξ−Bi|≤ε, their determinant gives

2𝐻𝜀≥𝑔gcd(𝑔,𝐷).2Hε≥ggcd(g,D).

This is a restriction on two independent forms in the divided lattice. For one nonzero integral form tending to zero, no additional product 𝐻𝜀 →0Hε→0 is required.

A collision must have a small nonzero real remainder

Counting residues within short intervals gives small differences. To keep a difference nonzero, one must also bound the number of selectors with the same residues and the same real value.

Theorem 4.9 (equal residues with close, distinct values). Let 𝐴,𝐵,𝐽A,B,J be finite sets and let 𝑓 :𝐴 →𝐵f:A→B, 𝑔 :𝐴 →ℝg:A→R and 𝜄 :𝐴 →𝐽ι:A→J. Suppose that each simultaneous fibre of (𝑓,𝑔)(f,g) has at most 𝑘k elements and that, for some 𝛿 >0δ>0,

𝜄(𝑥)=𝜄(𝑦)⟹|𝑔(𝑥)−𝑔(𝑦)|<𝛿.ι(x)=ι(y)⟹|g(x)−g(y)|<δ.

If |𝐵||𝐽|𝑘 <|𝐴||B||J|k<|A|, then some distinct 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝐴x,y∈A satisfy

𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑦),0<|𝑔(𝑥)−𝑔(𝑦)|<𝛿.f(x)=f(y),0<|g(x)−g(y)|<δ.

Proof. Partition 𝐴A by (𝑓,𝜄)(f,ι). Some cell has more than 𝑘k elements, so its 𝑔g-values cannot all agree. Two unequal values in that cell have the same residue vector and differ by less than 𝛿δ. ◻

Primitivity gives no useful bound on 𝑘k: repeated rows (1,0)(1,0) produce the same sum and remainder for every subset of a given size. The application below therefore needs a separate multiplicity estimate.

Fix positive integers 𝑛,𝐷n,D and 𝑀M primitive integer rows (𝐴𝑗,𝐵𝑗)(Aj,Bj), indexed by 0 ≤𝑗 <𝑀0≤j<M. Put 𝑒𝑗 =𝐴𝑗𝐹(3/2) −𝐵𝑗ej=AjF(3/2)−Bj and apply Theorem 4.9 to binary selectors, with

𝑓(𝜀)=∑𝑗𝜀𝑗(𝐴𝑗,𝐵𝑗)(mod𝐷),𝑔(𝜀)=∑𝑗𝜀𝑗𝑒𝑗.f(ε)=∑jεj(Aj,Bj)(modD),g(ε)=∑jεjej.

Let 𝑄Q be the number of attained residue vectors and let 𝑘k bound the simultaneous (𝑓,𝑔)(f,g) fibres. For a rank-two lattice generated by these rows, the preceding Smith formula gives 𝑄 ≤𝐷2/gcd(𝑔0,𝐷)Q≤D2/gcd(g0,D), where 𝑔0g0 is the gcd of the minors; it gives no bound on 𝑘k. The selector remainders span an interval of length 𝑇 =∑𝑗|𝑒𝑗|T=∑j|ej|. Subtract its minimum, multiply by 𝑛/𝐷n/D, and take floors. The resulting indices range from 00 to ⌊𝑛𝑇/𝐷⌋⌊nT/D⌋, and two remainders with the same index differ by less than 𝐷/𝑛D/n. Thus a sufficient inequality is

2𝑀>𝑄𝑘(⌊𝑛𝑇𝐷⌋+1).(1)(1)2M>Qk(⌊nTD⌋+1).

It yields a signed row sum divisible coordinatewise by 𝐷D, whose divided real remainder has absolute value strictly between 00 and 1/𝑛1/n. The residue-specific version is in the long record, Section 10.1. The multiplicity bound is what prevents a zero remainder; polynomial nonvanishing does not.

The remaining construction problem

The next question specifies the required integer forms, not an approximation family. Unrestricted, it is equivalent to irrationality of 𝐹(3/2)F(3/2); the long record, Section 10, proves the converse even with the stated index bounds and coefficient height exp⁡(𝑂(𝑛2))exp⁡(O(n2)). A method-specific problem must additionally fix its coefficient formulas, parameter set and permitted normalisations.

together with polynomial pairs (𝑈𝑛,𝑗,𝑉𝑛,𝑗) ∈ℤ[𝑋]2(Un,j,Vn,j)∈Z[X]2 for 0 ≤𝑗 <𝑀𝑛0≤j<Mn, each of degree at most the common degree bound 𝑊𝑛Wn, whose specialised integer rows are primitive:

satisfies the explicit analytic condition

Source comparisons and finite computations

Integer-base methods.

Vandehey treats signed coefficients in the digit argument ; Duverney and Tachiya prove linear-independence refinements [11]. Van Assche gives a little 𝑞q-Legendre construction . These integer-base methods are compared in the long record’s related-work section; they are not inputs to the rational specialisation in Section 2.

Coefficient moments.

The coefficient polynomials in [5] give a moment problem different from the remainder moments in Section 3. Long Section 3.3 treats it at fixed ranks only; the all-rank criterion of [15] is not addressed. Write 𝐴𝑁AN and 𝐵𝑁BN for the 𝑁 ×𝑁N×N Hankel matrices of the coefficients 𝛼𝑚,𝛽𝑚αm,βm in 𝑣∗𝑚 =𝛼𝑚𝐹(𝑝) −𝛽𝑚vm∗=αmF(p)−βm, where 𝑝 =1/𝑞p=1/q. Lean proves the finite-pencil proposition: for real 𝑝 >1p>1 and every rank 𝑁 ≤8N≤8, 𝐴𝑁AN is positive definite, all roots of det(𝑌𝐴𝑁 −𝐵𝑁)det(YAN−BN) are real and less than 𝐹(𝑝)F(p), and roots at adjacent ranks interlace non-strictly. It also proves the positivity of the leading Hankel determinants behind the first conclusion, through rank eight at every real 𝑝 ≥1p≥1. The other finite results are exact computations outside Lean, with their certificate lists and reproduction scripts in the long record: positivity of the shifted Hankel determinants through rank eight, complete polynomial contents through rank five and specified cyclotomic residue tests through rank eight. From these the long record proves a finite moment representation, and it discusses (𝑚!)3(m!)3 at the endpoint [16], formal continued fractions and finite quadrature [17][18]. None of these results asserts all-rank coefficient positivity or divisibility.

Functional equations.

Bell and Smertnig’s classification [9] excludes 𝑘k-Mahler equations for 𝐿(𝑧) =∑𝑛≥1𝜏(𝑛)𝑧𝑛L(z)=∑n≥1τ(n)zn when 𝑘 ≥2k≥2: there is no polynomial-coefficient relation among 𝐿(𝑧),𝐿(𝑧𝑘),…,𝐿(𝑧𝑘𝑑)L(z),L(zk),…,L(zkd) with a nonzero coefficient of 𝐿(𝑧)L(z). The single-base exclusion is also a Lean theorem, in the form that for every 𝑘 ≥2k≥2 no finite-dimensional ℚ(𝑧)Q(z)-subspace of ℚ((𝑧))Q((z)) containing 𝐿L is stable under 𝑧 ↦𝑧𝑘z↦zk. Long Section 10.3 explains this functional obstruction; it gives no irrationality statement for 𝐿(2/3) =𝐹(3/2)L(2/3)=F(3/2).

Rectangular exponent model.

Long Section 10.4 shows that within the rectangular two-function exponent model the threshold never exceeds the classical one-function margin, with equality only at the classical endpoint. Lean proves the bound for the rectangular exponent expression and the equality case for that bound. The bound concerns only that exponent model.

What is checked in Lean
  • Lean checks irrationality and the stated irrationality-exponent bound for rational bases in the exact Zudilin contour region, including every positive integral power of 31/431/4. The contour excludes 3/23/2.
  • For p>1 and 𝑁 ≤8N≤8, Lean checks positive definite coefficient matrices, real finite-pencil roots below F(p), and non-strict interlacing at adjacent ranks. Neither all-rank positivity nor irrationality at 3/23/2 follows.
  • That a literal coordinatewise transfer of the integer-base clearing argument forces a power-versus-linear inequality, and that this inequality is impossible at base three halves.
  • The exact denominator-cleared rational-base tail recurrence, including its forcing term.
  • That for every noninteger base with denominator at least two the forcing magnitude grows at least exponentially, while at denominator one it collapses to a bounded expression.
  • The complete elementary Archimedean height inequality used by the published Bundschuh-Väänänen criterion at base seven halves; the analytic irrationality theorem itself remains external.
  • Polynomial bounds on the doubled denominator exponents in the homogenised Padé construction, together with an exact gap identity.
  • The exact exterior-determinant elimination identity, and that rowwise contents scale the Padé errors, exterior determinant, and absolute determinant height by the same factors.
  • The exact Heine-Zudilin cone endpoint exponent arithmetic used to identify the bottom and top coefficient endpoints.
  • That homogeneous evaluation at (3,2) sees only the constant endpoint modulo three and the top endpoint modulo two, so unit endpoints obstruct common local factors.
  • That under unit top and constant endpoint hypotheses, a common multiplier of the two specialised coefficient channels is divisible by neither two nor three; the missing local gain must therefore survive primitive normalisation.
  • That vanishing of the higher bottom and top endpoint jets is exactly divisibility by the corresponding powers of three and two.
  • That the source integer-base ratio inequality implies a strictly negative scalar product-formula margin at three halves.
  • That the four-jet target has exact cardinality (3𝑅)2(2𝑆)2(3R)2(2S)2 and, for positive R, any family with n at least 4R+2S forces two distinct binary selectors to collide; their {-1,0,1} difference cancels all four endpoint jets.
  • That the rectangular Hermite-Pade threshold never improves on the classical one in the checked exponent model, with equality characterised exactly.
  • The exact 81/20081/200 height region: 31/431/4 and every positive power lie inside it and outside the earlier Bundschuh-Vaananen region, while 3/23/2 lies outside both.
  • At 𝑛 =0n=0, the Amdeberhan-Zeilberger q-Apery operator applied to Van Assche's moving diagonal has residual −𝑝(𝑝 −1)2(𝑝 +1)(𝑝5 +2𝑝4 +2𝑝3 +2𝑝2 +2)−p(p−1)2(p+1)(p5+2p4+2p3+2p2+2), which is strictly negative and nonzero for every real 𝑝 >1p>1.
What is not checked
  • The universal rational-base conjecture, including the case 3/23/2, remains open. The checked 31/431/4 power family settles one region and leaves that conjecture untouched.
  • The published analytic height theorem, which is cited and used as an external result and is not formalised here.
  • The all-scale Heine-Zudilin coefficient construction at rational base three halves; the primary source assumes an integer base.
  • A sufficiently large primitive-normalised, non-collapsed coefficient family meeting the checked 𝑛 ≥n≥ 4R+2S threshold at the required quadratic depths.
  • That one of the resulting bounded-coefficient collision vectors has a nonzero polynomial pair, lies outside the analytic remainder nullspace, and has sufficient local gain.
  • The elementary Padé pilot checks exponent arithmetic only; it lacks remainder positivity or decay and does not qualify the separate Zudilin contour result.
  • The n=0 q-Apéry residual gives no general recurrence, lattice, valuation, denominator, or irrationality result; it only blocks the named scalar transfer.
The formal record: 3 main results, 1 open obligation, 6 Lean modules, Comparator review

Main results

no-go result family: coordinatewise_corridor_no_go

The coordinatewise divisibility corridor is impossible at base 3/23/2.

This excludes one proof architecture and proves no irrationality statement.

locally proved result; novelty unassessed family: rational_base_tail_recurrence

The rational-base cleared tail obeys its exact first-order recurrence.

The recurrence is not derived from a rationality contradiction.

ErdosProblems.Erdos1049.rationalBaseClearedTailQ_succ
locally proved sharp model-specific no-go; novelty unassessed family: height_and_pade_arithmetic

For the explicit rectangular two-function exponent model, with real rho and sigma satisfying 0 ≤𝜌0≤ρ and 1 +𝜌 ≤𝜎1+ρ≤σ, the threshold equals 1/2 −1/𝜋21/2−1/π2 exactly when 𝜌 =0ρ=0 and 𝜎 =1σ=1.

This is a sharp no-go only for the explicit rectangular two-function model under the stated real hypotheses; it constructs no approximating polynomials or remainders and is not a universal Pade or Hermite-Pade no-go. It proves no irrationality at 3/23/2 or any general rational-base endpoint, and the analytic remainder/nonvanishing input remains untreated. No novelty, priority, significance, external-review, or endpoint claim is made; Erdős #1049 remains open.

ErdosProblems.Erdos1049.rectangular_hp_threshold_eq_classical_iff
